query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings, wear resistance is governed primarily by the load-induced dynamic amorphization that refines the coarse initial grain structure into an ultra‐nanocrystalline near-surface layer. This nanostructured layer, manifesting inverse Hall-Petch behavior, lowers the shear strength and friction coefficient during wear, thus enhancing wear performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase HEA coatings (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with a coarse-grained microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled mechanical deformation (e.g., via sliding wear tests) under inert (or ultra-high vacuum) conditions to induce dynamic amorphization at the surface.
generation.conditions: Wear tests conducted in a friction and wear rig under inert conditions to prevent oxidation, with systematic variations in applied load and sliding speed to trigger the transition from coarse to ultra-nanocrystalline surface states.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer from dynamic amorphization of the coarse-grained initial structure.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical stress, dynamic amorphization leads to grain refinement at the surface. This produces a nanostructured layer exhibiting inverse Hall-Petch behavior, characterized by a decrease in shear strength with reduced grain size. The refined layer results in lower friction coefficients and exceptional wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples that experience the controlled mechanically-induced transformation will show a near-surface nanocrystalline structure (detectable via STEM), a reduction in friction coefficient (around ~0.3) and minimal wear rates (~10–6 mm³/N-m), in contrast to untreated samples.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings with coarse-grained structure not subjected to controlled deformation, which would either not form the nanocrystalline layer or form it less effectively, thereby showing higher friction and wear rates.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected to hold over a range of mechanical loads and sliding speeds in inert or ultra-high vacuum environments where oxidation effects are minimized. Deviations are possible if environmental factors (e.g., oxidation) or HEA composition variations significantly alter the dynamic amorphization process.
generation.uncertainty: The quantification of the exact load threshold and rate of dynamic amorphization, as well as the influence of slight compositional variations in different HEA systems, remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coating samples with identical coarse-grained initial structures. Subject one set to controlled, high-load sliding wear tests under inert conditions designed to induce dynamic amorphization. Keep the other set as a control (minimal deformation). Characterize the near-surface grain structure (using STEM) and measure friction coefficients and wear rates for both sets.
measurements: Grain size distribution in the near-surface region (via STEM).
Friction coefficient measurements during wear tests.
Wear rate quantification (mm³/N-m) using profilometry or similar techniques.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If controlled deformation does not result in a statistically significant formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline layer, or if the treated samples do not exhibit the predicted lower friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
